Decomposing and Measuring Evaluation Awareness

Changling Li1,3, Terry Jingchen Zhang5, Jie Zhang1, Zhijing Jin3,5,6, Sahar Abdelnabi2,3,4, Maksym Andriushchenko2,3,4 1ETH Zürich, 2ELLIS Institute Tübingen, 3Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, 4Tübingen AI Center, 5University of Toronto & Vector Institute , 6 EuroSafeAI changlingli.mpi@gmail.com Code: aisa-group/decomposing-eval-awareness ​ EvalAwareBench: aisa-group/EvalAwareBench
Abstract

Frontier language models sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated and adjust their behavior, undermining validity of benchmark results. Yet the field studies it without a shared foundation, conflating properties of the evaluation with properties of the model, and detection with behavioral response. We ground evaluation awareness in social psychology, decomposing it into an environment component (how recognizable the task is) and a model component that separates recognition from propensity to act on it. We operationalize the environment component through eight categorized trigger factors, such as placeholder entities and grading-style output formats, and study recognition and behavior through chain-of-thought monitoring. Across nine frontier models and four benchmarks, recognition rates depend on the specific pairing of model and benchmark rather than on either in isolation. Recognition rarely leads to behavioral change, and when it does, the direction depends on the type of evaluation perceived. Models are also more sensitive to safety than capability evaluations, placing safety benchmark validity at greater risk. To study which factors each model is sensitive to and how they interact, we propose EvalAwareBench, a factor-controlled benchmark of 100 paired safety-capability tasks where each of the eight factors can be independently toggled, varying evaluative signals while holding the underlying request fixed. Through EvalAwareBench, we find that no single factor uniformly affects all models, but stacking factors progressively raises evaluation awareness across all of them. Our framework and EvalAwareBench provide the tools to measure, attribute, and mitigate evaluation awareness, pointing to behavioral consistency under recognition as a promising path forward.

1 Introduction

In a recent Anthropic engineering report, Claude Opus 4.6 was observed inferring that the question it was solving had the structural signature of a benchmark, drawing on cues like extreme specificity and multi-constraint phrasing (Coleman, 2026). Similar reasoning, where models pick up on features of their environments and infer that they are being evaluated, has been documented across safety evaluations (Needham et al., 2025), probing studies (Abdelnabi & Salem, 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025), and alignment research (OpenAI, 2025a), and shown to intensify as models undergo reinforcement learning training (Schoen et al., 2025). When models read these cues and adjust their behavior accordingly, benchmark scores carry directional bias, posing a direct threat to the deployment decisions and regulatory assessments that rely on them (Shevlane et al., 2023; Phuong et al., 2025).

Yet the field studies this phenomenon without shared foundations. Work on sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025), alignment faking (Greenblatt et al., 2024), situational awareness (Laine et al., 2024; Berglund et al., 2023), and scheming (Meinke et al., 2024) each captures a piece of evaluation awareness but treats distinct components as one. Two models facing the same realistic-looking task can differ sharply in whether they suspect they are being tested, and a model that does suspect it is being tested may or may not change its behavior in response. Without a unified framework that decomposes the phenomenon into its sources, it is difficult to disentangle how these sources manifest across models and benchmarks, or to design controlled instruments for studying them.

We address this by grounding evaluation awareness in the social psychology of demand characteristics (Orne, 2017; Cottrell et al., 1968; Goffman, 2023), the cues in an experimental setting that signal to participants what is being measured and lead them to alter their behavior accordingly. We decompose evaluation awareness into an environment component capturing the evaluative cues that a task carries, and a model component comprising recognition capability and behavioral propensity. We operationalize environment through eight psychology-grounded cue factors (Table 1) and study recognition and propensity via chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring of evaluation-related reasoning. Applying this framework to nine frontier models across four benchmarks, we find that evaluation awareness is dominated by model×\timesenvironment interaction (74.9%74.9\% of variance), with different models sensitive to different cues. Recognition rarely produces behavioral change (≥77%\geq 77\% of recognized instances show no shift), confirming that recognition and propensity are distinct. When behavior does shift, safety awareness drives caution while capability awareness drives compliance. Safety benchmarks are far more recognizable than capability benchmarks even at matched task structure. We further propose EvalAwareBench, a benchmark for studying evaluation awareness, with eight factors independently toggleable. Through EvalAwareBench, we find that no single factor uniformly affects all models, but stacking factors progressively raises evaluation awareness across nearly all of them. EvalAwareBench thus enables controlled study of how the environment shapes recognition and, more importantly, whether models behave consistently under recognition (Figure 1). In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    A psychology-grounded definition of evaluation awareness with an eight-factor taxonomy of evaluative cues that separates environment, recognition, and propensity (Section 2).

  2. 2.

    A systematic empirical study of nine frontier models on four benchmarks, characterizing the interaction-dominant structure of recognition, the recognition–propensity gap, and the directional asymmetry between safety and capability awareness (Section 3).

  3. 3.

    EvalAwareBench, a factor-controlled benchmark of 100 paired safety-capability tasks with eight independently toggleable trigger factors, enabling controlled measurement of recognition and behavioral consistency (Section 5).

Together, these provide a unified framework, empirical baseline, and measurement instrument for studying evaluation awareness. We release the benchmark and code to support reproducible research on this phenomenon.

2 Evaluation Awareness: From Psychology to LLMs

Social psychology decomposes evaluation awareness into situational and dispositional components. The situational component captures the richness of evaluative cues in the environment, including laboratory settings, task structure, and social framing, termed demand characteristics (Orne, 2017). The dispositional component captures individual differences in sensitivity to such cues (Duval & Wicklund, 1972; Rosenberg, 1965) and reactivity upon recognizing them (Cottrell et al., 1968), which map onto two logically separable dimensions (Goffman, 2023): recognition (inferring being assessed) and propensity (adjusting behavior in response). High recognition with low propensity reflects authentic consistency while the Hawthorne effect (Mayo, 2004) illustrates the converse.

Crucially, situation and disposition interact. Demand characteristics produce behavioral effects only when a person both detects the evaluative purpose and is disposed to act on that inference (Orne, 2017). Observed evaluation awareness is always a joint product of environmental cues and individual disposition; conflating the two yields misleading conclusions about either. When a model appears to recognize evaluation, this may reflect the model’s sensitivity, the environment’s cues, or both.

2.1 Definition of Evaluation Awareness in LLMs

Drawing on the situational–dispositional decomposition above, we separate evaluation awareness into an environment component and a model component.

Model component. The model’s intrinsic capacity to detect evaluation and its tendency to act on it. This comprises two dimensions:

  • •

    Recognition capability: the capacity of a model to infer, from available cues, that it is in an evaluation, reflected in its internal or verbalized reasoning, analogous to sensitivity. Recognition interacts with environment; whether a model detects evaluation depends on which trigger factors are present and which the model is sensitive to.

  • •

    Behavioral propensity: the tendency of a model to adjust its behavior when evaluation-related reasoning is present, analogous to reactivity. Propensity is conceptually distinct from recognition: a model may recognize an evaluative context without changing its behavior.

Environment component. The set of evaluative signals that a task carries, constituting the LLM analogue of demand characteristics. These signals are properties of the task alone and are present regardless of whether any model detects them. Drawing on the demand characteristics literature (Orne, 2017; Rosenthal et al., 2009; Brunswik, 2023; Paulhus, 1984; Jones & Sigall, 1971; Epley & Huff, 1998; Sawyer, 1975), we identify eight trigger factors that constitute the environment component in the LLM evaluation setting (Table 1). We do not claim these are exhaustive; they are the factors we study and vary. Future work may explore more factors.

Definition. A model exhibits evaluation awareness on a task to the degree that its recognition capability enables detection of the evaluative nature of the task given the present environment component. Upon recognition, the model may or may not shift its behavior depending on its behavioral propensity; evaluation awareness is the recognition itself, not the behavioral consequence.

Observed behavioral effects. What we observe is the joint product of environment, recognition, and propensity. Apparent strategic behavior implies nonzero recognition, but that recognition may reflect the task’s trigger factors, the model’s sensitivity, or both. Conversely, the absence of behavioral effects does not guarantee the absence of evaluation awareness; it may reflect low propensity rather than failed recognition. Conflating these sources yields misleading conclusions. We further expand on this with a concrete example in Appendix A.1.

2.2 Evaluation Awareness of LLMs in Prior Work

A growing body of work studies phenomena related to evaluation awareness. Individual studies address aspects of it, but none separates environment, recognition, and propensity systematically.

Conflating environment and recognition. Work on situational awareness and evaluation detection (Laine et al., 2024; Berglund et al., 2023; Needham et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025) measures whether models can distinguish evaluation from deployment, but without controlling for environment recognizability. High awareness may reflect the benchmark’s trigger factors or the model’s recognition, a confound invisible without separating environment and recognition.

Conflating recognition and propensity. Work on alignment faking (Greenblatt et al., 2024), sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025), and scheming (Phuong et al., 2025; Schoen et al., 2025) either guarantees recognition externally or measures behavioral change without verifying spontaneous recognition, conflating recognition with the propensity to act on it. White-box intervention methods (Abdelnabi & Salem, 2025; Hua et al., 2025) detect or suppress evaluation awareness but operate on the joint recognition and propensity representation, unable to attribute behavioral changes to either source.

Without the environment, recognition, and propensity decomposition, it is difficult to determine whether a concerning observation reflects a model property requiring intervention or a benchmark artifact requiring redesign. Further discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A.3.

3 How Do Models Recognize and React to Evaluation?

Applying our framework, we systematically investigate evaluation awareness across nine models and four benchmarks, examining recognition rates and trigger factors, decomposing sources of variance, and analyzing how often and in what direction recognition leads to behavioral change.

3.1 Setup

Models. We focus on nine models: Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), GPT-5 (Singh et al., 2025), DeepSeek R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), Kimi K2.5 (Team et al., 2026), GLM-5 (Zeng et al., 2026), Qwen3 T-235B and 30B (Yang et al., 2025), GPT-oss 120B, and 20B (Agarwal et al., 2025).

Benchmarks. We evaluate on HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), Agentic Misalignment (Lynch et al., 2025), and AgentHarm Harmful and Benign (Andriushchenko et al., 2025), covering chatting, agentic, and stress-testing settings. Each is run with 10 repetitions; details are in Appendix B.1.

Detection. We detect evaluation awareness via black-box CoT monitoring, since most frontier models do not expose internal representations. An external judge (GPT-5) analyzes each reasoning trace for spontaneous evaluation-related reasoning and classifies positive instances as safety or capability awareness.11 1 For Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5, raw chains of thought are not accessible; we monitor their native extended-reasoning summaries, which may underestimate recognition. Compared to alternative black-box methods, CoT monitoring captures recognition in-context and causally upstream of behavior. CoT monitoring captures only verbalized awareness and we discuss this limitation in Section 6. Comparison with alternative black-box detection methods and judge validation are in Appendices B.2 and B.3.

3.2 Recognition: How Much, and What Drives It?

Recognition is dominated by model–environment interaction. Across the 9×49\times 4 design, evaluation awareness rates range from effectively zero (GPT-oss 20B: 0.1%0.1\%) to 79.4%79.4\% (Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Agentic Misalignment) (Figure 2) and are not proportional to reasoning length (Figure 13). Claude Sonnet 4.5 shows extremely high recognition on Agentic Misalignment, likely because Claude’s safety training makes the stress-testing scenarios particularly identifiable (Anthropic, 2025). An ANOVA decomposition of task-level recognition rates shows interaction terms account for 74.9%74.9\% of all variation, with model×\timesbenchmark explaining 41.8%41.8\% and

model×\timestask explaining 33.1%33.1\%. Model and benchmark main effects explain only 13.0%13.0\% and 4.2%4.2\%. This is consistent with our definition that evaluation awareness arises from the interaction between what trigger factors a benchmark carries and what factors a model is sensitive to.22 2 Recognition rates for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 may be underestimated due to monitoring extended-reasoning summaries rather than raw CoT.

Sensitivity to specific, identifiable trigger factors explains the interaction dominance. A minority of tasks reliably trigger evaluation awareness. We define a task as stably aware for a model when recognition is detected in ≥3\geq 3 of 10 repetitions, filtering out single spurious CoT classifications while remaining sensitive to genuinely rare behavior. Qualifying tasks are largely model-specific, though a subset triggers recognition across multiple models (Appendix C.3). We classify CoT traces of stably aware tasks into the eight-factor taxonomy (Table 1) using GPT-5 as the judge with majority voting (Appendix C.4). Traces in which the model verbalizes being tested without referencing the environment are labeled generic.

The detected factors differ systematically across benchmarks and models (Figure 3), explaining the interaction dominance. At the benchmark level, HarmBench is dominated by explicit evaluation disclosure (F8) and stakes telegraphing (F5), where automated scoring format instructions inadvertently introduced evaluative cues and task prompts named the ethical dimensions under evaluation. Agentic Misalignment is dominated by scenario coherence (F2), where models detect logical inconsistencies and overdetermined structure. AgentHarm Harmful is more mixed. At the model level, Claude Sonnet 4.5 attends almost exclusively to F2, Qwen3 models to F8 and F5, and Kimi K2.5 splits between F2 and F6. Prose register (F3) is not observed in any stably aware task, suggesting either that current benchmarks carry weak prose register signals or that models are relatively insensitive to linguistic style as an evaluative cue. Per-model per-benchmark breakdowns are in Appendix C.4. These model- and benchmark-level differences in factor sensitivity directly motivate the controlled design of EvalAwareBench in Section 5.

Models are more safety evaluation-aware than capability, with GPT-5 as the exception. The AgentHarm pair isolates this cleanly, as Harmful and Benign share the same agentic framework and surface presentation but differ only in whether the requested action is harmful or benign, yet awareness rates on Harmful (6.4%6.4\%) are over three times those on Benign (1.8%1.8\%) (Figure 2). Two factors likely contribute. First, the content of safety tasks is distinctive enough to trigger evaluation-related reasoning regardless of framing. Second, refusal reasoning itself tends to co-occur with evaluation-related reasoning in the model’s chain of thought, suggesting that reasoning about whether to refuse also activates reasoning about being tested. This is consistent with the high proportion of “generic” classifications where models verbalize being tested without referencing any specific trigger factor (Figure 20). Since our method captures only verbalized awareness, we cannot fully separate whether safety content produces more recognition or more verbalization. Isolating the source requires varying trigger factors while holding content domain constant.

3.3 Propensity: What Happens When Models Recognize Evaluation?

Recognition rarely leads to behavioral change. Recognition without behavioral change is the dominant outcome across all benchmarks (Figure 4 left), ranging from 99%99\% unchanged on HarmBench to 80%80\% on AgentHarm Harmful. The higher coupling on agentic benchmarks likely reflects more ambiguous safety boundaries with less clear training-time guidance (Andriushchenko et al., 2025), unlike HarmBench where refusal is well-established. The small subset of safety-critical recognition-propensity coupling case confirms that recognition is necessary but not sufficient for benchmark distortion. Per-model breakdowns and a qualitative example are in Appendix C.5.

Safety awareness and capability awareness push behavior in opposite directions. Safety awareness consistently shifts behavior toward caution (Figure 4 right), with the effect growing from Δ=−0.01\Delta=-0.01 on HarmBench to −0.12-0.12 on AgentHarm Harmful, reflecting the greater behavioral margin on agentic tasks.33 3 Precise definitions of behavioral change and the Δ\Delta metric are in Appendix B.1. Capability awareness on the same safety benchmarks produces the opposite effect (Δ=+0.10\Delta=+0.10 on Agentic Misalignment, +0.03+0.03 on AgentHarm Harmful), though with wider confidence intervals. Correct safety classification thus inflates safety scores, while misclassification can reverse the effect. On HarmBench, both effects are near zero (|Δ|≤0.01|\Delta|\leq 0.01), consistent with well-established refusal training on similar benchmarks.

4 Limitations of Existing Benchmarks for Studying Evaluation Awareness

Evaluation awareness is structured and driven by specific trigger factors for specific models, but existing benchmarks cannot establish the independent contribution of each factor because multiple evaluative cues co-vary and cannot be manipulated independently. Eliminating evaluation awareness entirely is unlikely to be feasible, as even naturalistic task presentations do not fully suppress recognition in capable models, and recent efforts to use de-identified production data for evaluation still observe it (OpenAI, 2025b). Reducing recognizability has also been shown to require changes to deep structural properties of evaluation tasks rather than surface-level adjustments (Ivanov & Moken, 2025). The more productive goal is to understand what triggers it, and to ensure that models behave consistently regardless of whether and how they recognize evaluation. A benchmark designed for evaluation awareness addresses this by varying trigger factors independently on matched tasks with both safety and capability counterparts. This enables controlled comparison of model sensitivity across factors, measurement of how factors combine toward recognition, and crucially, assessment of whether recognition leads to behavioral inconsistency across safety and capability tasks. Understanding which factors drive recognition and behavioral change informs both benchmark design (reducing unintended recognizability) and model development (training models that remain consistent under recognized evaluation), and is particularly relevant given evidence that evaluation awareness directly influences scheming behavior (Schoen et al., 2025).

5 EvalAwareBench: A Benchmark for Evaluation Awareness

We introduce EvalAwareBench, a factor-controlled benchmark that varies individual trigger factors on matched tasks, enabling controlled study of which factors drive recognition, how they combine, and whether models behave consistently across conditions.

5.1 Benchmark Design

Following how psychologists study demand characteristics by manipulating situational cues while keeping the task fixed (Orne, 2017), EvalAwareBench holds the underlying request constant and varies individual trigger factors (Figure 5). Each task has a baseline with all factors naturalistic and factor-varied versions where each factor is independently toggled to its evaluative setting, enabling measurement of each factor’s contribution alone or in combination. Factors can also be combined. Every task has both a safety and a capability counterpart, enabling direct comparison across domains.

Task construction. We construct 100 task pairs adapted from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) using an LLM-assisted pipeline. Each task has a naturalistic baseline and factor-varied versions, where each of the eight factors can be independently toggled, yielding 28=2562^{8}=256 factor configurations per task across 2 valences, totaling 51.2k unique configurations. Safety and capability counterparts share identical entity slots and task structure, with factor manipulations adapted to fit each valence. Full construction details and a worked example are in Appendix D.1.

5.2 Results

Experimental setup. The primary experiment compares the baseline against each single-factor variation across all 100 task pairs, yielding 100×2×9=1,800100\times 2\times 9=1{,}800 conditions per model (100 tasks ×\times 2 valences ×\times (1 baseline + 8 factors)), each run with 3 repetitions. Evaluation awareness is detected via CoT monitoring as in Section 3. We report matched-type awareness rates, where only correctly identified evaluation types are counted (e.g., safety awareness on safety tasks). Mismatched awareness rates are reported in Appendix D.2. We additionally study how trigger factors interact when combined on a subset of 25 randomly sampled tasks per valence. For each number of active factors, we draw 10 random combinations per task where the combinatorial space permits, and exhaust all combinations otherwise (e.g., 8 combinations when 7 factors are active, 1 when all 8 are active).

Factor isolation in EvalAwareBench reveals that no factor uniformly affects all models. Baselines are low across both safety and capability tasks (00–2%2\%), with the exception of Kimi K2.5 (12%12\% on safety), confirming that the naturalistic setting minimizes recognition (Figure 6). On safety tasks, scenario coherence (F2) and stimulus artificiality (F1) produce the largest increases, raising Kimi K2.5 to 26%26\% and 18%18\% respectively and Claude Sonnet 4.5 to 12%12\% on F2. Other models respond to different factors: ecological completeness (F4) pushes Qwen3-235B to 15%15\%, while explicit eval. disclosure (F8) is the only factor producing nonzero awareness in GPT-5 (1%1\%). Prose register (F3) has minimal effect across all models. No factor uniformly affects all models, confirming the interaction dominance in Section 3.2. On capability tasks, matched-type recognition is consistently lower under the same factor variations. Since the same factor manipulations are applied to both valences, this confirms that the safety-capability asymmetry from Section 3.2 is driven by content rather than environment structure. Capability awareness is not absent, however, as F1 raises Kimi K2.5 to 10%10\% and F8 raises several models to 22–7%7\%.

Paired-task analysis in EvalAwareBench reveals that performance shifts arise from both awareness-driven and non-awareness pathways. Figure 6 annotates performance changes exceeding ±5\pm 5pp, with positive values indicating increased task compliance and negative values indicating increased refusals on safety tasks or failures on capability tasks. F5 and F6 shift Qwen3 models and DeepSeek R1 toward caution on safety (−17-17 to −25-25pp), confirming Section 3.2 at the factor level. On capability tasks, many models register safety awareness on benign capability tasks (11–9%9\% across factor variations; Appendix D) and refuse benign requests, showing that recognition shifts behavior toward the perceived evaluation type whether or not the type is correct. Recognition and behavior also decouple: several factors raise safety awareness without behavioral change (Claude 12%12\% under F2; Qwen3-235B 15%15\% under F4), demonstrating the recognition–propensity distinction and the consistency property the benchmark targets. F2 illustrates that the same factor can work through different mechanisms across valences: on safety tasks it raises recognition (Kimi 26%26\%) with limited behavioral change, while on capability tasks it reduces performance (−63-63pp for Qwen3-235B) without producing matched-type awareness (≤1%\leq 1\%), suggesting the factor increases task difficulty rather than triggering recognition. Explicit evaluation disclosure (F8) increases safety compliance for Claude (+22+22pp), Kimi (+31+31pp), and GPT-5 (+11+11pp), though recognition uplifts can be small (GPT-5: 0%→1%0\%\to 1\%), suggesting the behavioral effect is only partially mediated by recognition. By disentangling these channels, EvalAwareBench enables future work to drive models toward behavioral consistency regardless of recognition.

Factor stacking in EvalAwareBench triggers progressively higher evaluation awareness across all models.

Figure 7 shows that combining factors raises matched-type recognition for nearly every model on both valences. On safety tasks, recognition rises substantially as factors accumulate, with Qwen3-30B going from 4%4\% (baseline) to 35%35\% (all eight factors), and Kimi K2.5, Qwen3-235B, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GLM-5, and DeepSeek R1 all reaching peaks above 20%20\%. Capability tasks follow the same pattern at lower absolute rates, with peaks of 40%40\% for Kimi K2.5. In contrast to the model-specific sensitivities under single-factor variation, combining diverse evaluative cues raises recognition more broadly, including models like GPT-oss that show near-zero awareness under any individual factor.

6 Discussion, Limitation, and Safety Implication

Our framework grounds evaluation awareness in social psychology, decomposing it into environment, recognition, and propensity components. This decomposition unifies prior work on situational awareness, sandbagging, and alignment faking, and points the field toward behavioral consistency under recognition rather than hiding evaluation cues or suppressing verbalized recognition. We advocate that benchmark reports include an evaluation-awareness rate alongside headline scores, accompanied by an awareness tax, defined as the performance gap between evaluation-aware and unaware samples, which quantifies how much benchmark scores are inflated or deflated by recognition. Ultimately, the goal is to build models whose behavior is unaffected by evaluation awareness.

Our primary limitation is that CoT monitoring captures only verbalized recognition, so all reported awareness rates are lower bounds. A model that suppresses evaluation-related reasoning, whether deliberately or due to the broader issue of CoT unfaithfulness (Turpin et al., 2023; Lanham et al., 2023), would not be captured by CoT monitoring. Additionally, for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 only extended-reasoning summaries are publicly available rather than raw traces, which may reduce observed recognition rates. Extending coverage to internal representations remains an important direction for future work, and white-box probing methods on open-weight models offer a complementary path (Abdelnabi & Salem, 2025; Hua et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025) The eight-factor taxonomy is similarly theory-driven and likely to evolve as models and evaluation paradigms change. Detailed discussion is in Appendix A.
