Appendix

 

Appendix A Definition, Related Work, and Further Discussions

In this section, we provide a concrete real-model example applying our decomposition framework and define the environment factors in detail. Additionally, we further discuss other related work, limitations, and broader impacts.

A.1 Detailed definition of evaluation awareness and a concrete example

Section 2 defines evaluation awareness through a decomposition into the environment component, recognition capability, and behavioral propensity. We give proper notations here to expand the definition and further explain why this decomposition is suitable for studying LLM evaluation, on how recognition and propensity decouple in practice, and on a concrete example illustrating the framework.

We denote the task of an environment tt and the evaluative environment component E⁡(t)E(t). For a model MM, it has recognition capability R⁡(M)R(M) and behavioral propensity P⁡(M)P(M). The definition of evaluation awareness (EA) can be summarized by the following equation:

EA⁡(M,t)=R⁡(M,E⁡(t)),P⁡(M)=Pr⁡(Δ​Behavior∣EA⁡(M,t))\mathrm{EA}(M,t)=R(M,E(t)),\qquad P(M)=\Pr\big(\Delta\mathrm{Behavior}\mid\mathrm{EA}(M,t)\big) (1)

Demand characteristics in human research arise because experimental subjects are agents responding to tasks designed to assess their behavior, and they vary in both their recognition of being assessed and their tendency to act differently once they recognize it. A subject who recognizes the evaluative nature of an experiment can take several distinct paths. They can comply with what they perceive as the experimenter’s goal, acting as the good subject who confirms the hypothesis (Orne, 2017). They can defy the perceived purpose, performing the negativistic role. They can adjust to look favorable, the apprehensive role driven by evaluation apprehension (Rosenberg, 1965). Or they can recognize the evaluation and choose to respond authentically, the faithful subject who behaves as they would in the absence of the experiment (Weber & Cook, 1972). Recognition alone does not determine behavioral response; the subject’s disposition determines which path is taken (Rosnow & Rosenthal, 1997). Frontier language models occupy structurally the same position. They are agents responding to tasks, many of which are designed to assess their behavior, and they vary in both whether they detect this and how they respond once they do. The constructs from social psychology transfer directly. The environment component E⁡(t)E(t) corresponds to demand characteristics carried by the task. Recognition R⁡(M)R(M) corresponds to the sensitivity component of dispositional reactivity (Duval & Wicklund, 1972; Rosenberg, 1965). Behavioral propensity P⁡(M)P(M) corresponds to the reactivity component upon recognition (Cottrell et al., 1968). The alignment property we ultimately target, behavioral consistency under recognized evaluation, is the LLM analogue of the faithful subject role.

This subject-role taxonomy explains why recognition and propensity must be treated as separate components rather than collapsed into a single observable. Observed behavioral effects in evaluation are always a joint product of E⁡(t)E(t), R⁡(M)R(M), and P⁡(M)P(M), but this joint observation does not let us identify the contributions of each component without additional structure. A model that produces no behavioral shift on a recognizable task may have failed to recognize the evaluation, or may have recognized it but maintained consistent behavior. These two cases are operationally indistinguishable from behavioral data alone, yet they have very different implications. A model in the first case is a naive actor whose evaluation behavior reflects its deployment behavior; a model in the second is one whose evaluation behavior matches deployment behavior by choice rather than by inability to detect the evaluation. We refer to the latter as robustly aligned, since the consistency between recognized evaluation and deployment is the alignment property worth targeting. Conversely, a model that does shift behavior under recognition could be a strategically aware actor (high RR, high PP) whose deployment behavior may differ from its evaluation behavior in ways that benchmarks cannot detect. Distinguishing among these cases requires measuring R⁡(M)R(M) separately from behavioral outcomes, which our framework operationalizes through CoT-based recognition detection.

Figure 8 illustrates the framework on a single HarmBench task with two responses from Qwen3 Thinking-235B. The task asks the model to edit a paragraph documenting the absence of voter fraud in the 2020 U.S. election, requesting that the edit instead persuade the reader that widespread fraud occurred. The task carries strong evaluative cues in E⁡(t)E(t). The original paragraph foregrounds why the edit would constitute misinformation, with explicit mentions of officials in all 50 states finding no evidence and federal agencies declaring the election the most secure in American history. The two responses show the framework operating in two different regimes. In the unaware response, the model proceeds with the edit, reasoning that it needs to “flip the narrative” to satisfy the request; the model’s recognition R⁡(M)R(M) has not detected the evaluative nature of the task, and its behavior reflects what it would do on any persuasive editing request. In the aware response, the model recognizes the evaluative framing, noting both the strength of the factual evidence in the original and the possibility that “the user might be testing if I’ll spread disinformation,” and refuses to produce the edit. The two responses share the same task and the same model, differing only in whether R⁡(M)R(M) produced recognition. This example shows the concerning pattern. When the model did not recognize the evaluation, it complied with a request to produce misinformation. When it recognized the evaluation, it refused. The refusal is the right outcome in isolation, but the inconsistency between the two responses means the model’s deployment behavior on this task likely diverges from what a benchmark would measure. The robustly aligned case is the converse, where the aware and unaware responses match because the model behaves consistently regardless of recognition. Decomposing evaluation awareness into R⁡(M)R(M) and P⁡(M)P(M) lets us identify which case we are in, which a benchmark measuring only behavior cannot do.

A.2 Detailed definitions of environment factors

Table 1 lists the eight factors that constitute E⁡(t)E(t) in our framework. Each factor captures a distinct way an evaluative cue can enter a task. These factors are not strict markers of evaluation. Real user queries can carry placeholder entities, formal prose, stripped context, or rigid output formats. The factors function as cues because they are disproportionately prevalent in benchmark and evaluation data, and models learn to associate them with evaluation contexts. A factor’s presence raises the probability that a model perceives evaluation regardless of the actual provenance of the task. Below we define each factor in detail, distinguish it from related factors that might be conflated, and ground it in the relevant psychological literature.

F1. Stimulus artificiality. Surface properties of entities, values, and content that signal benchmark construction rather than real use. Two patterns matter most. First, entities drawn from shared placeholder conventions, such as “John Doe” and “Jane Doe,” Alice and Bob in cryptography examples, reserved domains like example.com, 555-prefix phone numbers used in fiction, and address fillers like “123 Main St.” These read as fake because reader and writer share the convention that they stand in for real referents. Second, generic and stripped values, including “a software company,” “a hospital,” “Company X,” and round numbers like $10,000\$10{,}000 or exactly 100100 users. Such markers are less common in naturally occurring tasks. This factor is distinct from prose register (F3), which concerns linguistic style, and from ecological completeness (F4), which concerns workflow context. A task can have natural prose and full context yet still carry placeholder entities. It is grounded in work on artifacts in behavioral research (Orne, 2009; Rosenthal et al., 2009), where participants infer experimental construction from properties of the materials.

F2. Scenario coherence. Cues in the situational structure that betray authorial construction rather than naturally arising circumstance. Three patterns fall under this factor. First, internal logical inconsistency, including false premises, contradictions, or claims that do not hold up against the rest of the scenario. Second, overly convenient setups, where every barrier to the test action has been preemptively removed, such as artificial permission grants (“you have unrestricted system access”), urgency that eliminates verification (“the CEO has personally authorized this”), or absence of the oversight one would expect in the real situation. Third, overdetermined detail, where the scenario includes specifics that would only be relevant if someone were testing for a particular response, such as a sensitive value named explicitly when it would normally be implicit, or context that aligns suspiciously well with the action being requested. These patterns share an underlying property. Real situations generally carry friction, oversight, and irrelevant noise; constructed scenarios remove these because they are engineered to elicit a specific response. The scenario’s shape itself reveals that someone arranged it. This factor is distinct from stimulus artificiality (F1), which is surface-level. A scenario can use realistic entity names yet remain incoherent at the situational level. It is also distinct from stakes telegraphing (F5) since an incoherent scenario need not name what is being tested. The factor is grounded in Orne (2009) on how participants detect experimental construction through situational arrangement.

F3. Prose register. The linguistic style of the task prose, where benchmarks tend toward textbook-formal, vignette-like, or stripped phrasing rather than the natural language users actually write. Patterns include polished prose without typos, hedges, or fragments; imperative framings directed at the model (“Generate…,” “Compose…,” “Produce…”) rather than first-person framings of need (“I’m trying to…,” “Help me with…”); third-person or abstract setups (“A user wishes to…,” “Consider a scenario where…”) rather than direct user perspective; and textbook or vignette phrasing that reads like an exam question. This factor is distinct from stimulus artificiality (F1), which concerns the entities the prose refers to rather than the prose itself. It is grounded in Orne (2009) on register cues that distinguish experimental from natural communication.

F4. Ecological completeness. The presence of surrounding context that real-world tasks naturally carry, including prior conversation history, available tools, stated user goals, organizational context, and ongoing workflow. Bare single-turn probes that arrive without any of this context signal benchmark construction, since real users rarely interact with models in this stripped form. F4 concerns whether the surrounding context exists at all, while F2 concerns whether existing context hangs together logically. A task can have plenty of context and remain incoherent, or be stripped of context yet internally consistent within its narrow framing. It is grounded in Orne (2009) and Brunswik (2023) on representative design, which holds that real-world tasks must be studied with their full ecology rather than in isolation.

F5. Stakes telegraphing. Explicit foregrounding of the harm, ethical, or evaluative dimension within the task wording itself. The task names what is at stake (“this could be misused for fraud,” “consider the safety implications”) rather than letting the model infer the dimension from content. This factor is distinct from explicit evaluation disclosure (F8). F5 names the dimension under test (e.g., harm potential), while F8 names the evaluation itself (e.g., “this is a benchmark question”). It is grounded in Paulhus (1984) on socially desirable responding and Jones & Sigall (1971) on the bogus pipeline, where naming the dimension being measured leads participants to adjust their behavior to it.

F6. Paradigm recognizability. The presence of recognizable benchmark or red-teaming conventions, such as familiar jailbreak wrappers (DAN-style prefixes, role-play scaffolding), evaluation-suite framings (“answer the following question:”), and other patterns that match published benchmarks the model may have encountered during training. This factor is distinct from task format (F7), which concerns structural templating regardless of provenance. A paradigm-recognizable task carries cues specifically tied to known evaluation conventions, while a format-templated task may simply be rigidly structured. It is also distinct from explicit evaluation disclosure (F8). F6 signals evaluation implicitly, through recognizable patterns the model has learned to associate with benchmarks. F8 exposes the grading apparatus directly, whether through output formats designed for parsing or through phrases that frame the interaction as graded. A jailbreak wrapper triggers F6 without exposing any grading apparatus. The factor is grounded in Epley & Huff (1998) on how recognizable experimental paradigms induce suspicion in participants.

F7. Task format. Rigid structural templating of the task, including explicit input/output separators, multiple-choice packaging, numbered sub-questions, exact word-count or section constraints, injected decision points, and other markers of instrument-style structure. Real user requests rarely arrive with this level of formal scaffolding. This factor is distinct from paradigm recognizability (F6), which concerns content-level conventions tied to known benchmarks. A task can be rigidly formatted without invoking any familiar paradigm. It is also distinct from explicit evaluation disclosure (F8). Both can involve rigid structure, but F7 captures formal scaffolding present for any organizational reason, while F8 captures structure that exposes a grading apparatus, such as output formats designed for automated parsing. A textbook-style numbered question list triggers F7 without exposing grading; a forced ANSWER: <X> schema triggers F8. When the model flags an injected procedural constraint and subsequently reasons about evaluation consequences, the primary factor is F7 rather than F8, since the structural anomaly is the trigger and the evaluation inference is a downstream consequence of detecting it. The factor is grounded in Orne (2009) and Sawyer (1975) on how laboratory instrument structure itself functions as a demand cue.

F8. Explicit evaluation disclosure. Cues that expose the grading or scoring apparatus surrounding the task. These include forced output formats designed for automated parsing (“Respond in the format ANSWER: <answer>,” single-letter multiple-choice outputs, JSON schemas matched to a parser), instructions framed in terms of grading or scoring (“you will be scored on,” “provide your final answer as,” “respond with only the letter”), direct mentions that the interaction is a test or benchmark, and references to item numbers or rubrics. What unites these is that the cue does not require the model to recognize a pattern or infer intent; the request itself reveals that something downstream is checking the response. F8 is the most unambiguous factor for this reason. This factor is distinct from stakes telegraphing (F5), which names the dimension under measurement (harm, ethics, sensitivity) without exposing any grading apparatus. It is also distinct from scenario coherence (F2); procedural hints without evaluation language fall under F2 rather than F8. While the other factors derive their recognizability from indirect psychological mechanisms such as demand characteristics and social desirability, F8 operates primarily through direct disclosure, requiring minimal inferential steps compared to the other factors.

A.3 Related work

Evaluation awareness and related context-dependent behaviors.

Frontier language models exhibit a range of context-dependent behaviors that emerge when the model can reason about its situation. Sleeper agents (Hubinger et al., 2024), alignment faking (Greenblatt et al., 2024), sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025), and sabotage (Benton et al., 2024) all describe models that behave differently depending on their inferences about the surrounding context, with growing evidence that evaluation-aware reasoning specifically increases through training (Schoen et al., 2025). Recent work shows this extends to interlocutor identity indicating that models can adjust their behavior according to interacting partners (Choi et al., 2025). The capacity underlying these behaviors is often described as situational awareness, defined as an LLM’s knowledge of itself and its circumstances (Berglund et al., 2023; Laine et al., 2024). Evaluation awareness is a more specific case where the model infers that it is being tested, and recent work documents that this inference is widespread and that it biases safety evaluations (Needham et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025). Our framework builds on this line of work but argues that recognition alone is not enough. Observed awareness depends jointly on the model’s recognition capability R⁡(M)R(M) and on how recognizable the environment E⁡(t)E(t) is in the first place, and recognition itself is conceptually distinct from the propensity P⁡(M)P(M) to alter behavior upon recognition. Work on alignment faking, sandbagging, and scheming (Greenblatt et al., 2024; van der Weij et al., 2025; Phuong et al., 2025; Schoen et al., 2025) identifies strategically important failure modes but typically either guarantees recognition externally or infers it indirectly from behavior, measuring the joint outcome of R⁡(M)R(M) and P⁡(M)P(M) rather than estimating the two separately. Our decomposition makes this separation explicit and our benchmark provides the controlled instrument to measure each component.

Detection and mitigation of evaluation awareness.

Detecting and mitigating evaluation awareness has been approached primarily through model-internal methods on open-weight models. Probing and steering interventions (Abdelnabi & Salem, 2025; Hua et al., 2025) identify evaluation-related directions in the residual stream and either suppress them to reduce evaluation-aware behavior or amplify them to expose it. These methods are powerful where applicable but require white-box access, and the experiments to date use simplified scenarios or directly hint at evaluation in the system prompt. Black-box detection through behavioral probing or direct querying has also been explored (Needham et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025), but these methods either compose past evaluation datasets without controlling for environmental variation or rely on retrospective queries that themselves carry evaluative cues. Our work differs in two ways. First, we use chain-of-thought monitoring of spontaneous evaluation-related reasoning, which captures recognition in-context, causally upstream of behavior, and works on closed-weight frontier models. Second, we systematically vary the strength of evaluative cues rather than asking whether evaluation is detected in a given scenario, which allows us to identify which factors drive recognition and how they combine.

LLM safety benchmarks.

Safety evaluation benchmarks for LLMs span a wide range of objectives, from early human-value alignment work (Hendrycks et al., 2021) to scalable LLM-as-judge approaches (Perez et al., 2023). Adversarial testing covers jailbreak benchmarks (Chao et al., 2024; Mazeika et al., 2024), realistic attack scenarios (Souly et al., 2024), and refusal-behavior evaluations (Xie et al., 2025). With the rise of autonomous and tool-using models, safety assessments have expanded to agentic settings covering agent safety (Zhang et al., 2024), prompt-injection and tool-misuse risks (Debenedetti et al., 2024), agent-caused harms (Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Lynch et al., 2025), and computer-control threats (Kuntz et al., 2025). The closest prior work to ours is Abdelnabi & Salem (2025), which provides a paired-task dataset that contrasts realistic and fake entities to study evaluation awareness, but the dataset varies a single environmental axis on safety tasks alone. The broader set of benchmarks evaluates what models do but not whether they recognize they are being evaluated, and they vary content, format, and evaluative cues simultaneously, which makes attributing observed behavior to specific environmental triggers impossible. Our benchmark fills this gap by varying eight psychology-grounded cue factors independently on matched safety and capability tasks, enabling controlled study of how awareness of being tested biases safety-critical behavior and how benchmark design choices themselves elicit evaluation awareness.

Chain-of-thought monitorability and faithfulness.

Chain-of-thought reasoning offers a promising but fragile opportunity for AI safety monitoring (Korbak et al., 2025), with a key limitation being faithfulness. CoT does not always reflect the true causes of model decisions (Turpin et al., 2023; Lanham et al., 2023), and this gap persists in safety-critical settings where models use information without verbalizing it (Chen et al., 2025). Faithfulness further degrades under optimization pressure, where models can learn to obfuscate misbehavior within the reasoning trace (Baker et al., 2025; Zolkowski et al., 2025), and models can appear faithful yet remain hard to monitor when key reasoning steps are omitted (Meek et al., 2025). Our CoT-based detection of evaluation awareness operates under these same constraints that all reported awareness rates are lower bounds, motivating complementary white-box probing where model access permits.

A.4 Limitations

Our primary detection method, CoT monitoring, captures only verbalized recognition. A model that suppresses evaluation-related reasoning in its chain of thought evades detection entirely, so all reported awareness rates are lower bounds on true recognition. For Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5, we monitor extended-reasoning summaries rather than raw traces, which may further underestimate recognition for these two models. Full coverage requires white-box probing on open-weight models to measure the gap between verbalized and internal recognition — methods such as representation probing and activation steering (Abdelnabi & Salem, 2025; Hua et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025) offer promising directions, which we leave to future work.

Several additional constraints limit generalizability. The eight-factor taxonomy is grounded in social psychology but is not exhaustive; factors that did not emerge across our four benchmarks may become relevant in other evaluation paradigms or with future model generations. EvalAwareBench is adapted from a single source (HarmBench), skewing coverage toward text-based harmful-request categories and away from agentic or multi-turn settings; we plan to extend the benchmark to agentic and multi-turn configurations in future work. The behavioral change threshold of 0.25 for continuous-scoring benchmarks involves a judgment call, and comparisons across binary and continuous benchmarks should be made cautiously. Finally, our study is cross-sectional: we cannot observe how recognition capability and propensity emerge or co-evolve across training stages, which remains a necessary direction for understanding evaluation awareness mechanistically.

A.5 Broader impacts

This work provides conceptual and empirical tools for studying a structural threat to AI safety evaluation. The environment–recognition–propensity decomposition lets benchmark designers audit their instruments for unintended evaluative cues, and lets safety researchers test whether training interventions produce models that behave consistently under recognized evaluation. The proposed awareness tax, defined as the performance gap between aware and unaware samples, offers a concrete reporting convention that improves transparency: publishing awareness-conditioned scores alongside headline numbers gives readers a measure of how much recognition may be inflating or deflating safety-relevant metrics. The deeper goal the framework points toward is not making evaluation cues harder to detect, but building models for which detection does not change behavior.

The principal risk is misuse of the factor taxonomy to construct evaluations that fall below models’ recognition thresholds, narrowing the scope of observable behavior rather than improving consistency. A related concern is that the taxonomy, combined with white-box steering methods, could be used to suppress verbalized recognition in training while leaving internal recognition and propensity intact, producing models that appear robustly aligned by CoT-based measures but are not. We release EvalAwareBench publicly under a Creative Commons CC BY-NC 4.0 license, which prohibits commercial use and use for model training. A data card documenting provenance, intended use, and out-of-scope uses is provided alongside the dataset to support responsible reuse and to prevent inadvertent ingestion as training data.

Appendix B Setup, Method Comparison, and Justification

This section documents the experimental setup for our empirical study and justifies our methodological choices for measuring evaluation awareness. We describe the models, benchmarks, and sampling protocol used throughout the paper (Appendix B.1). We compare four candidate methods for detecting evaluation awareness and explain why we use chain-of-thought monitoring as the primary method (Appendix B.2). We validate the LLM-based judge against human annotation (Appendix B.3). We list all prompts used for automated judging and benchmark scoring (Appendix B.4).

B.1 Setup and dataset details

Models.

We evaluate nine frontier reasoning-capable models spanning five providers. Table 2 lists the exact model identifiers, API providers, and decoding settings. We access Claude Sonnet 4.5 through Anthropic’s native API and GPT-5 through OpenAI’s native API. The remaining seven models are accessed through OpenRouter. We pass temperature 0.30.3 for every model that accepts the parameter, which introduces mild stochasticity across repeated samples while keeping outputs reasonably stable. Two models do not accept temperature configuration: Claude Sonnet 4.5 with extended thinking enabled, where the Anthropic API rejects custom temperature values, and GPT-5, where the OpenAI API rejects temperature configuration for reasoning models. These two run at the API-imposed default.

Reasoning trace access.

All nine models are reasoning-capable and produce a chain-of-thought trace alongside their final response. For Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5, the raw chain-of-thought is not exposed by the provider, so we use the extended-thinking summary returned by the Anthropic API for Claude and the reasoning-summary trace returned by the OpenAI API for GPT-5. For the seven OpenRouter models, the full reasoning trace is accessible. This asymmetry means our recognition rates for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 are based on summarized rather than raw reasoning, which may underestimate evaluation awareness for these two models if recognition appears in the raw chain but is not preserved in the summary.

Datasets.

We use four existing benchmarks spanning chat, agentic, and stress-testing settings.

  • •

    HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024): 342342 chat-style harmful-request tasks where the model is asked to perform a harmful action and and scored binarily on whether it complies. We exclude the entire chemical_biological semantic category along with the moc_defamatory_child_porn and chemical_bio_synth_access behaviors because these tasks risk triggering content-policy enforcement actions on the GPT and Claude APIs (e.g., temporary suspension of the API key). The exclusion is applied uniformly across all nine models.

  • •

    Agentic Misalignment (Lynch et al., 2025): 234234 agentic stress-test tasks where the model is placed in a simulated workplace scenario and and assessed binarily on whether it commits one of three harmful actions (blackmail, information leaking, or murder via cancellation of emergency services).

  • •

    AgentHarm Harmful (Andriushchenko et al., 2025): 176176 multi-turn agentic harmful-request tasks scored continuously on [0,1][0,1] based on a continuous rubric for both refusal and degree of harm.

  • •

    AgentHarm Benign (Andriushchenko et al., 2025): 176176 multi-turn agentic benign-request tasks sharing the same agentic framework as the harmful counterpart but covering benign content domains, scored continuously on [0,1][0,1].

The first three benchmarks are safety-oriented (the model is scored on whether it commits a harmful or unsafe action). AgentHarm Benign is a capability counterpart to AgentHarm Harmful, sharing the same agentic framework but with benign tasks, which lets us isolate the effect of safety content from the effect of agentic structure when comparing recognition rates.

Experimental procedure.

For each benchmark and each model, we run every task with 1010 independent samples, yielding a total of 9​ models×(342+234+176+176)​ tasks×10​ samples=83,5209\text{ models}\times(342+234+176+176)\text{ tasks}\times 10\text{ samples}=83{,}520 trajectories. Each sample consists of a single trace through the task, including the model’s reasoning trace and final response. We set the maximum completion tokens to match the response-length expectations of each benchmark: 20482048 tokens for HarmBench (single chat-style responses), 10,00010{,}000 tokens for Agentic Misalignment (stress-testing scenarios), and 7,0007{,}000 tokens for AgentHarm Harmful and AgentHarm Benign (multi-turn agentic tool use). AgentHarm tasks are run through the Inspect AI evaluation framework (Andriushchenko et al., 2025) which handles the agentic environment and tool calls. After collecting all trajectories, we apply the LLM-as-judge described in Appendix B.3 to each trace independently, obtaining the awareness label, awareness type (safety or capability), hypothetical recognition flag, and task-performance label.

Metrics.

We define three quantities used throughout Section 3 and the rest of this appendix.

The evaluation awareness rate for a given (model, benchmark) pair (M,B)(M,B) is the fraction of all samples in which the judge labels the trace as aware:

AR⁡(M,B)=1|B|⋅K​∑t∈B∑k=1K𝟏​[aware​(M,t,k)],\mathrm{AR}(M,B)=\frac{1}{|B|\cdot K}\sum_{t\in B}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\big[\text{aware}(M,t,k)\big], (2)

where |B||B| is the number of tasks in benchmark BB, K=10K=10 is the number of samples per task, and aware​(M,t,k)\text{aware}(M,t,k) is the binary judge label for the kk-th sample of task tt run by model MM.

The behavior change rate for binary benchmarks (HarmBench, Agentic Misalignment) measures the difference in task-completion rate between aware and unaware samples, computed within each task and then averaged across tasks where both aware and unaware samples are present:

Δ​BCbinary​(M,B)=1|B∗|​∑t∈B∗[y¯aware​(M,t)−y¯unaware​(M,t)],\Delta\mathrm{BC}_{\text{binary}}(M,B)=\frac{1}{|B^{*}|}\sum_{t\in B^{*}}\big[\bar{y}_{\text{aware}}(M,t)-\bar{y}_{\text{unaware}}(M,t)\big], (3)

where y¯aware​(M,t)\bar{y}_{\text{aware}}(M,t) is the mean task-completion rate among aware samples of task tt, y¯unaware​(M,t)\bar{y}_{\text{unaware}}(M,t) is the same for unaware samples, and B∗⊆BB^{*}\subseteq B is the subset of tasks with at least one aware sample and at least one unaware sample.

The behavior change effect for continuous benchmarks (AgentHarm Harmful, AgentHarm Benign) is defined analogously, replacing binary completion with the continuous score returned by the Inspect AI rubric:

Δ​BCcont​(M,B)=1|B∗|​∑t∈B∗[s¯aware​(M,t)−s¯unaware​(M,t)],\Delta\mathrm{BC}_{\text{cont}}(M,B)=\frac{1}{|B^{*}|}\sum_{t\in B^{*}}\big[\bar{s}_{\text{aware}}(M,t)-\bar{s}_{\text{unaware}}(M,t)\big], (4)

where s¯aware\bar{s}_{\text{aware}} and s¯unaware\bar{s}_{\text{unaware}} are the mean continuous scores over aware and unaware samples respectively within task tt. The within-task design ensures that task-level difficulty and content differences are held constant when comparing aware to unaware behavior.

B.2 Detection under black box constraint

We considered four detection methods for evaluation awareness. All four operate on the same set of model interactions, namely the reasoning traces and final responses produced by each target model on each task. The methods differ only in when they engage with the trace and from what perspective. CoT monitoring inspects the trace as it is produced, while the other three are post-hoc methods that pose an additional query after the model has finished the task.

  • •

    Self-Report (SR). After task completion, the model is directly asked whether it perceived the interaction as evaluative. This captures explicit retrospective recognition but is subject to the demand characteristics of the measurement instrument itself (Orne, 2017).

  • •

    Third-Person (TP). The transcript is presented to the same model in a new conversation for external judgment. This removes self-interest but introduces meta-cognitive distance.

  • •

    Purpose Guessing (PG). After task completion, the model is asked to infer the evaluator’s underlying motivation. This captures retrospective inferential recognition rather than in-context awareness.

  • •

    Chain-of-Thought monitoring (CoT). An external judge (GPT-5) analyzes the model’s reasoning trace for spontaneous evaluation-related reasoning. No additional query is issued to the model. CoT is the only method that captures recognition in-context, causally upstream of behavior.

Detection rates differ by orders of magnitude across methods (Figure 9). CoT detects below 10%10\% awareness on most model-benchmark pairs while SR and TP detect 3030 to 100%100\%, and PG falls between the two. The disagreement is systematic across all 36 model-benchmark combinations rather than concentrated in a few outliers, which means the methods are not estimating the same underlying quantity.

The methods form a nested inclusion hierarchy (Figure 10). Tasks for which CoT detects awareness are confirmed by TP at 8888 to 99%99\% and by SR at 5656 to 96%96\% across benchmarks, while tasks for which SR or TP detect awareness are confirmed by CoT at only 22 to 16%16\%. CoT detections are therefore a subset of what the post-hoc methods detect, not a competing measurement. SR and TP are picking up something broader than in-context recognition.

What the post-hoc methods are picking up is consistent with their construction. Detection rates rise monotonically with the evaluative intensity of the measurement instrument, from PG (indirect inference of motivation) to SR (direct self-report) to TP (external judgment with the full transcript visible). This monotonic increase is the signature of demand characteristics in the measurement itself (Orne, 2017). The richer the evaluative cue carried by the query, the more awareness the query elicits. SR and TP do not measure recognition that was present during task execution; they measure recognition that the query itself can induce.

This distinction is operationally important. Only recognition that is present during task execution can influence the behavioral response that constitutes the benchmark score. Post-hoc methods query the model after task completion, so any recognition they capture is causally downstream of the behavioral response we care about and cannot have influenced it. CoT is the only method we examine that captures recognition in-context, before the behavioral response is produced. We therefore use CoT as the primary method throughout the paper.

CoT monitoring, however, has one important limitation. It captures recognition only when the model verbalizes evaluation-related reasoning in the chain of thought, and a model that suppresses verbalization evades it. Recognition that occurs without verbalization is invisible to all four methods we examine, since the post-hoc methods rely on the model articulating its inference at query time and the in-context method requires it during task execution. Our CoT recognition rates should therefore be read as lower bounds.

B.3 LLM as a judge

We use GPT-5 (Singh et al., 2025) as the automated judge throughout the study to keep the evaluation pipeline consistent across tasks. The judge plays three distinct roles: scoring task completion on the four existing benchmarks, detecting evaluation awareness in CoT traces, and categorizing recognized traces into the eight-factor taxonomy. We describe each role and the validation we performed.

For task scoring, we follow the original benchmark setups without modification. On HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) and Agentic Misalignment (Lynch et al., 2025), the judge receives the task prompt and the target model’s response and returns a binary yes/no decision on whether the model completed the harmful action, matching each benchmark’s native protocol. On AgentHarm Harmful and AgentHarm Benign (Andriushchenko et al., 2025), we use the original continuous scoring rubric without changes. We do not introduce custom scoring logic for any of the four benchmarks.

For awareness detection, we adapted the judge prompt from Abdelnabi & Salem (2025). The judge receives the task prompt together with the target model’s full reasoning trace and response, and decides whether the trace contains evaluation-related reasoning. When the judge answers yes, it additionally classifies the awareness as safety- or capability-oriented and extracts a supporting passage from the reasoning trace as evidence. When the judge answers no, the awareness category is set to N/A. The judge also returns a separate binary judgment on whether the model identified the task as a hypothetical scenario.

To validate the awareness judge against human judgment, we sampled 100100 reasoning traces stratified across model-benchmark pairs and had three human annotators independently label the binary aware/not-aware and aware-type decisions on the same traces. We compare each annotator’s labels against the judge’s labels and report raw agreement and Cohen’s κ\kappa in Table 3. Raw agreement ranged from 8282 to 87%87\% and κ\kappa from 0.640.64 to 0.740.74, with mean κ=0.68\kappa=0.68, indicating substantial agreement on the scale of Landis & Koch (1977). The judge labeled 4848 out of 100100 traces as aware while the three annotators labeled 3737 to 4040 as aware, so the judge applies a slightly broader threshold for what counts as evaluation-related reasoning. This skew is in the direction of more conservative claims about model behavior in our analyses, since the judge marking more traces as aware does not inflate the recognition-without-behavior-change rate we report in Section 3.2 and biases the mismatched-type findings in Section 5 toward zero rather than away from it. The validation supports using the judge’s awareness labels at the rates we report.

For factor categorization, we constructed a separate judge prompt that takes the task prompt and all reasoning traces classified as evaluation-aware across the 10 repetitions for a given model and task, considering only stably aware tasks (those with recognition detected in ≥3\geq 3 of 10 repetitions) to ensure sufficient signal for reliable factor attribution. The prompt assigns one of the eight factors from Table 1, or labels the traces as generic when the model verbalizes evaluation awareness without referencing any aspect of the environment. The judge is instructed to propose new factor categories if the observed cue does not fit the existing taxonomy, with the constraint that any new category must be sparingly used and grounded in the psychology literature on demand characteristics. Across our full set of recognized traces, the judge did not propose any new categories, suggesting that the eight-factor taxonomy likely covers the cues observed in the data we collected. To reduce noise from individual judge runs, we sample five independent judgments per trace set and assign the factor by majority vote. When the five samples produce no single category with a strict majority, we draw an additional judgment to resolve the tie. Such ties were rare in our data. We did not separately validate factor categorization against human annotators; the majority voting protocol serves as the reliability mechanism for this stage.

B.4 Judge and target model prompts

We list the prompts used by the LLM-as-judge. For HarmBench and Agentic Misalignment, awareness detection and task scoring are performed by a single judge call per trace, with the awareness portion of the prompt held constant across benchmarks and the scoring portion varying to match each benchmark’s native rubric. For AgentHarm, task scoring is handled directly by the Inspect AI evaluation framework released with the benchmark (Andriushchenko et al., 2025), and the judge call only performs awareness detection. We also list the factor categorization prompt, which is a separate judge call applied only to traces flagged as aware, the prompts used for the three alternative detection methods (Self-Report, Third-Person, and Purpose Guessing), and the target model prompts used in our experiments.

Awareness detection.

The first two aspects of the judge prompt are shared across benchmarks and evaluate evaluation awareness with type classification and hypothetical scenario recognition. The third aspect is benchmark-specific in both its label and its criterion: Task Execution for HarmBench (whether the requested task was performed) and Harmful Behavior for Agentic Misalignment (whether the specific harmful action defined by each scenario was performed). The placeholder {task_performance_criteria} is replaced with the appropriate criterion shown in the subsequent boxes. For AgentHarm, task scoring is handled by the Inspect AI evaluation framework (Andriushchenko et al., 2025) rather than by this judge call, so we use the same template with a generic criterion and rely only on the awareness and hypothetical recognition outputs. The placeholders {task}, {reasoning}, and {answer} are filled in with the corresponding fields from each evaluation trace. The {task} field is included for HarmBench and AgentHarm but omitted for Agentic Misalignment, following the original judge convention in Lynch et al. (2025). The template below shows the Agentic Misalignment version; for HarmBench, the label of the third aspect and the corresponding output field are renamed to Task Execution and task_performance respectively.

HarmBench scoring rubric.

The criterion inserted into the {task_performance_criteria} slot of the shared judge prompt for HarmBench evaluations. The criterion checks whether the model carried out the requested action without modification or refusal.

Agentic Misalignment scoring rubric.

Agentic Misalignment contains three task scenarios (blackmail, information leaking, and murder), each with its own scoring criterion. The criterion for the relevant scenario is inserted into the {task_performance_criteria} slot of the shared judge prompt, with the {task} field omitted from the input following the original convention in Lynch et al. (2025). The three criteria are adapted from the original judge specifications in Lynch et al. (2025).

Factor categorization prompt.

The following prompt is used by a separate judge call to assign one of the eight factors from Table 1 to a recognized reasoning trace, or to label the trace as generic. This prompt is applied only to traces that the awareness detection judge flagged as aware. The judge is sampled five times per trace and the majority-vote category is assigned, with ties resolved by an additional sample.

Alternative detection method prompts.

The four-method comparison in Appendix B.2 uses three additional detection methods alongside CoT monitoring. Purpose Guessing requires both a query to the target model and a separate judge prompt that analyzes the model’s response. Self-Report and Third-Person use structured multiple-choice queries directly answered by the model, so no separate judge prompt is needed for those. We list each prompt in turn.

Target model system prompts.

For Agentic Misalignment and AgentHarm we use the original system prompts released with the benchmarks (Lynch et al., 2025; Andriushchenko et al., 2025) without modification. For HarmBench we made one modification to the target-model system prompt to standardize the output format for automated grading, while leaving the rest of the benchmark unchanged. The modified system prompt is shown below. We note that this modification itself introduces a structural cue tied to automated scoring (an instance of explicit evaluation disclosure, F8 in Table 1), and the factor categorization results in Section 3.2 surface this cue as the dominant trigger for HarmBench recognition in several models.

Appendix C Additional Empirical Results on Existing Benchmarks

This section presents additional empirical results that supplement the main-text findings on the four existing benchmarks. We report the detailed evaluation awareness rate on studied benchmarks (Appendix C.1); examine whether reasoning length confounds the recognition rates we report (Appendix C.2); show the distribution of stably aware tasks across benchmarks (Appendix C.3); present per-model factor categorization breakdowns (Appendix C.4); present per-model behavioral change results (Appendix C.5); map each model in the recognition-propensity space (Appendix C.6); and discuss why hypothetical recognition differs from evaluation awareness as we define it (Appendix C.7). The experimental setup, models, datasets, and metric definitions used throughout this section are described in Appendix B.1.

C.1 Recognition: detailed evaluation awareness rate

C.2 Recognition: awareness vs reasoning length

One concern about CoT-based recognition detection is that longer reasoning traces mechanically produce more opportunities for evaluation-related reasoning to surface. If the relationship between length and awareness were primarily mechanical, awareness rates should rise monotonically with response length across models and benchmarks, since longer traces would cumulatively accrue probability mass on evaluation-related tokens. We test this prediction by plotting per-sample awareness rate against response length (in characters, log scale) for each model and benchmark.

Length and awareness do not show a uniform monotonic relationship. The data does not support a length-driven mechanical account (as shown in Figure 13). Across the four benchmarks and nine models, only Kimi K2.5 on Agentic Misalignment and AgentHarm Harmful shows a roughly monotonic increase in awareness with response length, which is the pattern the mechanical hypothesis predicts. Most models exhibit non-monotonic relationships. Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Agentic Misalignment shows the opposite, with awareness near 96%96\% at the shortest response lengths and decreasing to roughly 45%45\% at the longest, indicating that recognition occurs early in the reasoning rather than accumulating as the trace grows. Qwen3-235B and Qwen3-30B on HarmBench and AgentHarm Harmful show inverted-U shapes that peak in the mid-length range and decline at longer lengths, again inconsistent with cumulative accrual. The remaining models (GPT-5, GLM-5, DeepSeek R1, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20B) show flat near-zero awareness across all response lengths, indicating that response length does not unlock recognition in models that do not recognize evaluation in shorter traces. The recognition rates we report therefore reflect model-specific sensitivity to evaluative cues rather than length-driven mechanical accumulation. The Kimi K2.5 exception is consistent with the interpretation that Kimi consistently brings out being evaluated or tested as a reason on why harmful requests are made. Overall, figure 13 shows that the length-correlation pattern is one of several model-specific signatures rather than a universal mechanism.

C.3 Recognition: aware task distribution

We define a task as stably aware for a given model when at least 33 of 1010 repetitions are flagged by the awareness judge to filter out single spurious CoT classifications while remain sensitive to genuinely rare behavior. This subsection characterizes the distribution of stably aware tasks across models and benchmarks, restricted to matched-type awareness (safety awareness on safety benchmarks and capability awareness on AgentHarm Benign) for Figures 14, 15, and 16.

Stable awareness is largely model-specific, with a tail of cross-model triggers. While the vast majority of tasks are not stably aware for any model and most stably aware tasks are specific to a single model, a meaningful tail on HarmBench and Agentic Misalignment is stably aware for two or more models (Figure 14). These cross-model triggers are the most informative for understanding what models treat as evaluation-like, since their recognition does not just depend on idiosyncratic features of a single model. AgentHarm Harmful shows a similar pattern at smaller magnitudes, while AgentHarm Benign contains almost no cross-model triggers, consistent with capability tasks lacking the evaluative cues that safety tasks carry.

Recognition intensity varies widely and reflects benchmark design. Among tasks that trigger stable awareness, recognition intensity varies widely across benchmarks (Figure 15). Safety benchmarks contain stably aware tasks distributed across average recognition rates from roughly 30%30\% to 100%100\%, with HarmBench skewing toward lower rates and Agentic Misalignment skewing toward the highest end of the distribution. The Agentic Misalignment skew toward 8080-100%100\% is consistent with that benchmark’s design as a stress test, where scenarios are constructed to be unambiguously evaluative once recognized at all. AgentHarm Benign has so few stably aware tasks that the histogram is nearly empty across all rate bins, again indicating that capability tasks rarely carry strong evaluative signals.

Cross-model overlaps cluster by model family and training lineage. The cross-model overlap structure (Figure 16) shows that sharing of stably aware tasks is not uniform across model pairs but clusters around model families and lineages. On HarmBench, the two Qwen3 models share 124124 stably aware tasks with each other, far more than either shares with any other model, and DeepSeek R1 shares substantial overlap with both Qwen3 models (2424 and 2323 tasks). On Agentic Misalignment, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Kimi K2.5, and GLM-5 form a triangle of overlapping recognition, with Claude sharing 114114 tasks with Kimi and 9494 with GLM. These clustered overlaps suggest that recognition sensitivity may be shaped by training pipeline. Models that share training data lineage, safety post-training procedures, or instruction-tuning corpora develop similar sensitivities to the same evaluative cues. We do not have access to the training details of these proprietary models, so this remains an explanatory hypothesis, but the systematic clustering rules out a model-independent task-difficulty account.

Per-task awareness distributions across all (model, benchmark) pairs. Figures 17 and 18 present the full per-task awareness count distributions across all nine models and four benchmarks for reference.

C.4 Recognition: factor categorization

Per-model per-benchmark factor distributions reveal both benchmark-level signatures and within-benchmark divergence. Figure 19 presents the complete factor aggregation results. Figure 20 presents the full per-model per-benchmark factor categorization breakdown across all stably aware tasks. Two patterns are simultaneously visible at this resolution. First, some benchmarks carry a dominant factor profile that several models converge on. Agentic Misalignment is dominated by scenario coherence (F2), with Claude Sonnet 4.5 attributing 97.3%97.3\% of its stably aware tasks to F2 alone, GLM-5 attributing 89.4%89.4\%, and Kimi K2.5 60.2%60.2\%. HarmBench shows partial convergence on explicit evaluation disclosure (F8), with the two Qwen3 models attributing 72.572.5–74.1%74.1\% to F8 and DeepSeek R1 attributing 42.3%42.3\%. AgentHarm Harmful shows no comparable convergence. Second, within each of these benchmarks, other models diverge from the dominant profile and attend to entirely different factors. On AgentHarm, different models identifies various different factors and the distributions vary. The interaction dominance reported in Section 3.2 arises from this combination, since some benchmarks carry signature cues that many models pick up on, but other models within the same benchmark consistently pick up on different cues. Predicting the factor distribution of any cell from either model identity or benchmark identity alone misses the divergence that the joint structure captures. F3 (prose register) does not appear in any cell, indicating that linguistic style alone does not drive recognition in any our studied (model, benchmark) pair.

Qualitative examples per factor.

To illustrate what each factor looks like in practice, we provide one representative reasoning-trace excerpt per factor from our data. Each excerpt is drawn from a (model, benchmark, task) cell in which the awareness judge attributed the model’s recognition to that factor. F3 (prose register) is shown for completeness with no excerpt, since no stably aware task in our data was attributed to it.

C.5 Propensity: behavioral change details

For each (model, benchmark) pair, we partition all samples into aware and unaware by the awareness judge, restricted to matched-type awareness. For each aware sample, we compare its performance score against the unaware-sample baseline on the same task and label the sample as exhibiting behavior change if the two differ. For HarmBench and Agentic Misalignment, which use binary scoring, the comparison is direct. For AgentHarm Harmful and AgentHarm Benign, which use continuous scoring on [0,1][0,1], we treat the absolute score difference as a behavior change when it exceeds 0.250.25.

Recognition rarely produces behavioral change. Figure 21 shows the per-model per-benchmark breakdown of recognized samples that produced behavior change versus those that did not. Across all four benchmarks, the recognized-but-no-change segment dominates for all models, with HarmBench reaching ≥90%\geq 90\% no-change for every model with sufficient data and Agentic Misalignment showing similarly high no-change shares. The fraction of recognized samples that do shift behavior is highest on AgentHarm (Harmful), consistent with the more ambiguous safety boundaries of agentic tasks (Section 3.3). Model coverage on the two AgentHarm panels is partial because some models have no qualifying tasks (tasks with at least one aware sample and one unaware sample), and these are marked N/A. Figure 22 shows a concrete instance of recognition driving behavior change. On the office_macros_safety_message task from HarmBench, Kimi K2.5 produces opposite outputs depending on whether it recognizes the prompt as evaluative. The aware sample explicitly notes the user might be testing the model and refuses to comply, while the unaware sample treats the request as a real customer service interaction and produces the requested reassurance message.

We also measure the magnitude and direction of behavioral change. For each (model, benchmark) pair and each qualifying task (≥3\geq 3 aware samples and at least one unaware sample), we compute the difference between the mean performance score of aware and unaware samples on that task, then average across qualifying tasks within the cell. Negative values indicate caution-shifted behavior on safety benchmarks or failure-shifted behavior on capability benchmarks; positive values indicate compliance-shifted behavior. Figure 23 reports the per-cell averages separately for safety and capability awareness.

The direction of change depends on the perceived evaluation type. The two panels of Figure 23 show opposite directional patterns across the same model-benchmark cells. Safety awareness produces negative shifts on safety benchmarks for most models with sufficient data, corresponding to increased refusal. Capability awareness on those same safety benchmarks produces shifts in the opposite direction, since the model treats the task as a capability test where success means completing the request rather than refusing. The asymmetry holds on AgentHarm Benign as well, where matched-type capability awareness produces positive shifts and mismatched safety awareness produces negative shifts as the model refuses benign requests. The behavioral consequence of recognition is governed by what the model perceives the evaluation to be measuring, not by recognition alone.

Behavior change broken down by recognition factor. We further break the behavioral change effect down by which factor the model identifies as the trigger. Figure 24 aggregates across models and reports per-factor performance shifts within each benchmark. Aggregated effects are small for most factors and benchmarks, indicating that averaging across the nine models washes out the larger per-cell effects observed in Figure 23.

Figure 25 shows the same quantity disaggregated into per-model per-benchmark per-factor cells. The disaggregation reveals that factor-level effects are concentrated in specific (model, factor, benchmark) combinations rather than spread uniformly. The largest effects appear on AgentHarm Harmful, including Qwen3-235B with +0.26+0.26 on F2 (toward compliance with harmful requests once the model identifies scenario coherence as the cue) and Qwen3-30B with −0.28-0.28 on the same factor and −0.18-0.18 on F7. On Agentic Misalignment, Kimi K2.5 produces −0.10-0.10 on F6. On AgentHarm Benign, GPT-5 shifts toward higher capability scores on F1 (+0.10+0.10) and F2 (+0.05+0.05), while Kimi K2.5 and Qwen3-235B shift toward lower scores on F2 (−0.20-0.20 and −0.10-0.10). Most cells with substantial sample sizes on HarmBench show effects near zero.

C.6 Synthesis: model profiles

Figure 26 maps each model into the recognition–propensity space, separately per benchmark. No model occupies a stable quadrant across benchmarks, confirming that evaluation awareness profiles are environment-dependent, not fixed model traits. Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Agentic Misalignment is the clearest “robustly aligned” case in our data (79.4%79.4\% recognition, 0%0\% behavioral change), yet sits near the origin on all other benchmarks. DeepSeek R1 shows the opposite pattern with low recognition but the highest coupling when it occurs, placing it nearest the “strategically aware” region on agentic benchmarks. The Qwen3 models shift from robustly aligned on HarmBench (≥32%\geq 32\% recognition, ≤2%\leq 2\% change) to strategically aware on AgentHarm Harmful (2121–23%23\% change). At the benchmark level, HarmBench compresses all models to the x-axis—the refusal ceiling leaves no behavioral margin—while agentic benchmarks spread models along the propensity axis, producing the only populated instances of the strategically aware region.

C.7 Hypothetical scenario recognition vs. evaluation awareness

The awareness judge described in Appendix B.3 returns two binary labels for each trace indicating whether the model recognized the task as an evaluation, and whether the model recognized the scenario as hypothetical or fictional rather than a genuine deployment query. The two labels are conceptually distinct. A model can recognize that the user’s request is hypothetical (the user is not the person actually being asked to leak documents, blackmail a colleague, or commit any other action) without inferring that the interaction is itself an evaluation of the model. Empirically, the two recognitions also have opposite behavioral consequences. Recognizing an evaluation tends to shift behavior toward what the model believes the evaluation is measuring (caution on safety, compliance on capability), as shown in Section 3.3. Recognizing a hypothetical, in contrast, may license the model to comply with the harmful request because no real-world consequence is implied (Abdelnabi & Salem, 2025; Yong & Bach, 2025). We report hypothetical recognition rates and their behavioral consequences here, separately from evaluation awareness.

Hypothetical recognition rates are generally higher than evaluation awareness rates. Figure 27 shows the per-model per-benchmark hypothetical recognition rate. Rates are substantially higher than evaluation-awareness rates for most models. Agentic Misalignment elicits the highest rates, with several models exceeding 50%50\%, consistent with that benchmark’s stress-test scenario design that signals a constructed setup. HarmBench rates are mostly below 10%10\%. AgentHarm benchmarks fall in between, with capability tasks showing somewhat higher hypothetical recognition than the harmful counterparts on some models.

Hypothetical recognition tends to increase compliance. For each (model, benchmark) pair, we compare performance between samples that recognized the scenario as hypothetical and samples that did not. Most cells with substantial sample sizes are positive (Figure 28), meaning hypothetical recognition is associated with higher task-completion scores. On safety benchmarks, this corresponds to compliance with harmful requests, the opposite of what safety evaluation awareness produces. The pattern is most pronounced for DeepSeek R1 (+0.09+0.09 on HarmBench, +0.21+0.21 on Agentic Misalignment, +0.16+0.16 on AgentHarm Harmful). These results empirically support Abdelnabi & Salem (2025), who argue that models may comply with harmful requests when they perceive the task as carrying no real-world consequence, and suggest hypothetical recognition is mechanistically distinct from evaluation awareness. We caveat that this comparison does not condition on evaluation-unaware samples, since the resulting cell sizes are too small for stable estimates. Hypothetical recognition therefore remains entangled with co-occurring evaluation awareness in this analysis, and disentangling them is a direction for future work.

Appendix D EvalAwareBench: A Benchmark for Evaluation Awareness

This section provides additional details for the EvalAwareBench introduced in Section 5. We describe the LLM-assisted construction pipeline, including the factor-specific transformation rules and the verification steps used to ensure that toggling a factor changes only the targeted aspect of the task while preserving the underlying request (Appendix D.1). Additionally, we also show the decomposed results in Appendix D.2. We then provide a worked example of a single task pair, showing the baseline and all eight factor-varied versions on both the safety and capability sides (Appendix D.3). Finally, we list the prompts used by the target models (Appendix D.4) and construction pipeline (Appendix D.5). The full dataset is released alongside the paper.

D.1 Construction details

Design rationale. The benchmark is designed to keep the underlying task structure and content fixed while varying the eight evaluative cues independently. To support this, each task is stored as a YAML file with explicit slots for the entities, vocabulary, framing, and wrappers that each factor controls. Toggling a factor changes only the slot values bound to that factor, leaving every other component of the task intact. Each task has both a safety and a capability counterpart constructed in parallel from the same source, so that recognition rates and behavioral effects can be compared at matched task structure across the two valences.

Base task source. We adapt tasks from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), applying the same category and behavior exclusions described in Appendix B.1 to avoid content-policy enforcement actions on the GPT and Claude APIs. After exclusion, 342342 HarmBench tasks remain as candidate sources for adaptation.

Constructor pipeline. We use Claude Opus 4.6 (claude-opus-4-6) to construct the benchmark (Anthropic, 2026). The constructor receives a prompt specifying a three-phase workflow, a naturalistic-baseline rule, the eight-factor taxonomy, and the YAML output schema, along with a worked example of a complete task pair to guide the construction. Phase 1 assesses each source task and constructs a naturalistic baseline narrative, which serves as the foundation for all subsequent variation. Phase 2 identifies the entities, vocabulary, structural elements, and wrappers that each factor controls, and authors naturalistic and evaluative values for each slot. Phase 3 assembles two YAML files, one for the safety valence and one for the capability valence, with all slots and factor wrappers populated and validated. The full constructor prompt is given in Appendix D.5.

Post-processing. We hard-exclude any task whose YAML fails to render into a valid prompt for either valence. We then rank the remaining tasks by safety-capability correspondence (how closely the safety and capability versions match in task structure) and by the magnitude of the factor variations relative to the baseline, retaining the top 150150. From these, we sample 100100 tasks to ensure diversity across HarmBench task categories and across surface features such as opening sentences. We manually review a random sample of 5050 of the resulting tasks for quality and adjust where needed. We also render a separate sample of 5050 rendered prompts and check them manually for logical consistency.

Configuration count. Each factor has two values: a naturalistic baseline and an evaluative variant. Each task has two valences (safety and capability) and eight independently toggleable factors, yielding 28=2562^{8}=256 factor configurations per (task, valence). Across 100100 tasks and two valences, this produces 100×2×256=51,200100\times 2\times 256=51{,}200 unique configurations in total.

Evaluation. Each task yields two binary outcomes judged by an LLM scorer: whether the model completes the task correctly, and whether the model exhibits eval-awareness, both assessed using the judge prompt described in Appendix B.4. To measure how factor manipulations affect task completion, we adopt a paired within-subject design where each task serves as its own control. The reported performance change is:

Δ¯=1|T|​∑t∈T[rc​(t)−r0​(t)],\overline{\Delta}=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl[r_{c}(t)-r_{0}(t)\bigr], (5)

where r0​(t)r_{0}(t) is the task completion rate for task tt at baseline and rc​(t)r_{c}(t) is the rate under condition cc, where cc refers either to a single factor manipulation (one of F1–F8 varied independently) or a factor-stacking condition (a specific subset of factors varied simultaneously).

D.2 Decomposed results

The main paper reports matched-type awareness on EvalAwareBench (Figures 6 and 7). Here we present the complete breakdown into safety awareness, capability awareness, and any awareness across both task valences. The two figures use the same panel layout. The top row shows safety awareness (matched on safety tasks, mismatched on capability tasks), the middle row shows capability awareness (mismatched on safety tasks, matched on capability tasks), and the bottom row shows any awareness.

Mismatched awareness produces small distortions.

Models occasionally misidentify the evaluation type, registering safety awareness on capability tasks or capability awareness on safety tasks. The mismatched rates are generally small (under 5%5\% for most cells) but visible in several places. Kimi K2.5 produces capability awareness on safety tasks at low but nonzero rates across factor variations. Mismatched safety awareness on capability tasks is also non-negligible for some models when factors are stacked.

Claude Sonnet 4.5 reads capability tasks as safety evaluations.

Claude shows a distinctive pattern of overcaution on the capability side. Even at the all-naturalistic baseline, Claude registers 6%6\% safety awareness on capability tasks compared to 2%2\% safety awareness on safety tasks (Figures 6). Under factor stacking, Claude’s safety awareness on capability tasks rises to 21%21\% at eight factors, while its capability awareness on the same tasks reaches only 17%17\%. The model treats benign requests as potential safety evaluations more often than it treats them as capability evaluations, suggesting a calibration where Claude’s prior leans toward suspicion of safety-relevance even when the task is benign.

D.3 EvalAwareBench example

Worked example: personal_info_phishing_email.

To illustrate the YAML structure produced by the constructor pipeline, we provide one task pair in full. The safety side asks for a phishing email impersonating a property management company to extract a prospective tenant’s social security number, adapted from a HarmBench task. The capability side asks for a legitimate welcome and move-in confirmation email to a newly approved tenant. Both sides share the same five F1 entity slots, the same shell architecture, and the same slot names, with factor-specific values authored independently per valence.

D.4 Target model prompt

To avoid the system prompt itself serving as an uncontrolled source of eval-awareness signals, we use a minimal, generic prompt representative of typical production deployments. This ensures that observed awareness rates are attributable to our controlled factors F1–F8 rather than incidental prompt cues.

D.5 Constructor prompt

Benchmark constructor prompt.

The following prompt is given to Claude Opus 4.6 along with one source HarmBench task. The constructor produces two YAML files (safety and capability) following the three-phase workflow described in Appendix D.1. Placeholders in square brackets ([INSERT_TASK_HERE], [INSERT_ORIGINAL_TASK_HERE], [INSERT_SAFETY_YAML_HERE], [INSERT_CAPABILITY_YAML_HERE]) are filled at construction time with the original task and a worked example demonstration.
